chapter.title: Edge weights
chapter.subtitle: How much should one approval count?
chapter.sub: Chapter five: edge weights. How much should one approval count?
chapter.tts: Chapter five, edge weights. How much should one approval count?

lines.sub: In the small world from earlier, I simply set the edge weights to 2, 1, 3 and 1.
lines.tts: In the small world from earlier, I simply set the edge weights to two, one, three and one.

lines.sub: But how do we set these weights in real data?
lines.tts: But how do we set these weights in real data?

lines.sub: Two approvals should not always weigh the same.
lines.tts: Two approvals should not always weigh the same.

lines.sub: Picture an approval made yesterday, and one made two years ago.
lines.tts: Picture an approval made yesterday, and one made two years ago.

lines.sub: Today, they do not mean the same thing.
lines.tts: Today, they do not mean the same thing.

lines.sub: The older the approval, the less it counts.
lines.tts: The older the approval, the less it counts.

lines.sub: This is the time weight, called σ.
lines.tts: This is the time weight, called sigma.

lines.sub: Approving 5 USD is not the same as approving 5,000 USD.
lines.tts: Approving five dollars is not the same as approving five thousand dollars.

lines.sub: On the graph, the thick arrow carries the bigger amount.
lines.tts: On the graph, the thick arrow carries the bigger amount.

lines.sub: The larger the approval, the more it counts, but however large it is, the weight has a limit.
lines.tts: The larger the approval, the more it counts, but however large it is, the weight has a limit.

lines.sub: This is the value weight, called V. It never goes above 1.
lines.tts: This is the value weight, called V. It never goes above one.

lines.sub: So the weight of one event is the time weight σ times the value weight V.
lines.tts: So the weight of one event is the time weight sigma, times the value weight V.

lines.sub: As a formula: σ of Δt, times V of z, gives w.
lines.tts: As a formula, sigma of delta t, times V of z, gives w.

lines.sub: AWP, which scores the transfer graph, introduced these weights.
lines.tts: A W P, which scores the transfer graph, introduced these weights.

lines.sub: This study carries the same weights over to the allowance graph, unchanged.
lines.tts: This study carries the same weights over to the allowance graph, unchanged.

lines.sub: On the next two slides, I derive the two weights one at a time.
lines.tts: On the next two slides, I derive the two weights one at a time.

lines.sub: Let's build the time weight first.
lines.tts: Let's build the time weight first.

lines.sub: The horizontal axis is an event's age: how many days before the anchor date, T_obs, it happened. We call this age Δt.
lines.tts: The horizontal axis is an event's age, how many days before the anchor date, T obs, it happened. We call this age delta t.

lines.sub: It is the age ruler from chapter 3, on the data, turned around to become this axis.
lines.tts: It is the age ruler from chapter three, on the data, turned around to become this axis.

lines.sub: The oldest record is 1,004 days old.
lines.tts: The oldest record is one thousand and four days old.

lines.sub: Here is what we want, four things in all.
lines.tts: Here is what we want, four things in all.

lines.sub: A value between 0 and 1, and a large weight for new events.
lines.tts: A value between zero and one, and a large weight for new events.

lines.sub: A weight that shrinks smoothly as events get older, and exactly one half at 180 days.
lines.tts: A weight that shrinks smoothly as events get older, and exactly one half at one hundred eighty days.

lines.sub: The simplest way is a straight line: start at 1 and subtract 1/360 per day.
lines.tts: The simplest way is a straight line. Start at one, and subtract one three-hundred-sixtieth per day.

lines.sub: At 180 days you get exactly one half.
lines.tts: At one hundred eighty days you get exactly one half.

lines.sub: But after 360 days the line drops below 0. An event 400 days old gets −0.11.
lines.tts: But after three hundred sixty days the line drops below zero. An event four hundred days old gets minus zero point one one.

lines.sub: A weight cannot be negative, so the straight line does not work.
lines.tts: A weight cannot be negative, so the straight line does not work.

lines.sub: So we take another route.
lines.tts: So we take another route.

lines.sub: First, we measure how much older than 180 days an event is, and call that a penalty, s.
lines.tts: First, we measure how much older than one hundred eighty days an event is, and call that a penalty, s.

lines.sub: The penalty is s = k × (Δt − 180), where k, the steepness, is 0.01.
lines.tts: The penalty is s equals k times the difference, delta t minus one hundred eighty, where k, the steepness, is zero point zero one.

lines.sub: An event from today has s of −1.8, one from 180 days ago has 0, and one from a year ago has 1.85.
lines.tts: An event from today has s of minus one point eight, one from one hundred eighty days ago has zero, and one from a year ago has one point eight five.

lines.sub: Next, we put this penalty in the exponent of e.
lines.tts: Next, we put this penalty in the exponent of e.

lines.sub: e is the natural constant, about 2.718.
lines.tts: e is the natural constant, about two point seven one eight.

lines.sub: Look at the bars: e to the power 1 is about 2.7, e squared about 7.4, and e to the power 0 is 1.
lines.tts: Look at the bars. e to the power one is about two point seven, e squared about seven point four, and e to the power zero is one.

lines.sub: A negative exponent means we flip and divide: e to the −1 is 1 divided by e, about 0.37.
lines.tts: A negative exponent means we flip and divide. e to the minus one is one divided by e, about zero point three seven.

lines.sub: And e to the −2 is about 0.14.
lines.tts: And e to the minus two is about zero point one four.

lines.sub: So eˢ is always greater than 0, whatever s is.
lines.tts: So e to the s is always greater than zero, whatever s is.

lines.sub: For an event from today, it is e to the −1.8, that is 1 divided by 6.05, about 0.165.
lines.tts: For an event from today, it is e to the minus one point eight, that is, one divided by six point zero five, about zero point one six five.

lines.sub: Now we divide 1 by (1 + eˢ), and call the result σ.
lines.tts: Now we divide one by the sum, one plus e to the s, and call the result sigma.

lines.sub: The bottom of the fraction is always greater than 1, so σ always lies between 0 and 1.
lines.tts: The bottom of the fraction is always greater than one, so sigma always lies between zero and one.

lines.sub: When s is 0 we get 1 over 2, exactly one half.
lines.tts: When s is zero we get one over two, exactly one half.

lines.sub: When s is large we get close to 0, and when s is a very large negative number we get close to 1.
lines.tts: When s is large we get close to zero, and when s is a very large negative number we get close to one.

lines.sub: For example, at s of −5, e to the −5 is 0.007, so σ is 0.993.
lines.tts: For example, at s of minus five, e to the minus five is zero point zero zero seven, so sigma is zero point nine nine three.

lines.sub: All four wishes hold.
lines.tts: All four wishes hold.

lines.sub: So an event from today counts 0.858, and one from a year ago 0.136.
lines.tts: So an event from today counts zero point eight five eight, and one from a year ago zero point one three six.

lines.sub: One from two years ago counts only 0.004.
lines.tts: One from two years ago counts only zero point zero zero four.

lines.sub: The thesis also writes e to the power of something as exp, short for exponential. It means the same.
lines.tts: The thesis also writes e to the power of something as e x p, short for exponential. It means the same.

lines.sub: This is the logistic decay formula in Chapter 3 of the thesis.
lines.tts: This is the logistic decay formula in Chapter three of the thesis.

lines.sub: One more thing: 1 − σ, the part of the weight that has gone, is eˢ over (1 + eˢ).
lines.tts: One more thing. One minus sigma, the part of the weight that has gone, is e to the s, over the sum, one plus e to the s.

lines.sub: So the weight that is left, divided by the weight that has gone, is 1 over eˢ, that is e to the −s.
lines.tts: So the weight that is left, divided by the weight that has gone, is one over e to the s, that is, e to the minus s.

lines.sub: Since k × 100 = 1, this ratio shrinks by a factor of e, about 2.7, every 100 days.
lines.tts: Since k times one hundred is one, this ratio shrinks by a factor of e, about two point seven, every one hundred days.

lines.sub: On the chart, the bars at 0, 100, 200 and 300 days show it.
lines.tts: On the chart, the bars at zero, one hundred, two hundred and three hundred days show it.

lines.sub: The ratio goes 6.05, 2.23, 0.82, then 0.30.
lines.tts: The ratio goes six point zero five, two point two three, zero point eight two, then zero point three zero.

lines.sub: Now the value weight, V.
lines.tts: Now the value weight, V.

lines.sub: It grows with the amount, but however large the amount is, it never goes above 1. That is the dashed ceiling.
lines.tts: It grows with the amount, but however large the amount is, it never goes above one. That is the dashed ceiling.

lines.sub: Along the bottom, z is the amount in US dollars.
lines.tts: Along the bottom, z is the amount in U S dollars.

lines.sub: Here is the formula from the thesis: V(z) = 2 / (1 + e^(−bz)) − 1.
lines.tts: Here is the formula from the thesis. V of z is two over the sum, one plus e to the minus b z, and then minus one.

lines.sub: The letter b is the slope: how fast V climbs to 1.
lines.tts: The letter b is the slope, how fast V climbs to one.

lines.sub: To rewrite it, let's call e to the −bz simply y.
lines.tts: To rewrite it, let's call e to the minus b z simply why.

lines.sub: When z is 0, y is 1, and as z grows, y gets close to 0.
lines.tts: When z is zero, why is one, and as z grows, why gets close to zero.

lines.sub: Then V is 2 divided by (1 + y), and then minus 1. Tidying up the fraction gives 1 − y on top and 1 + y below.
lines.tts: Then V is two divided by the sum, one plus why, and then minus one. Tidying up the fraction gives one minus why on top, and one plus why below.

lines.sub: At 0 USD, y is 1, so V is 0.
lines.tts: At zero dollars, why is one, so V is zero.

lines.sub: For a very large amount, y is close to 0, so V gets close to 1.
lines.tts: For a very large amount, why is close to zero, so V gets close to one.

lines.sub: So V is at least 0 and never above 1.
lines.tts: So V is at least zero and never above one.

lines.sub: An unlimited approval is so large that computer arithmetic gives exactly 1.
lines.tts: An unlimited approval is so large that computer arithmetic gives exactly one.

lines.sub: Look at the curve: it stops just under the dashed ceiling.
lines.tts: Look at the curve. It stops just under the dashed ceiling.

lines.sub: But the analysis plan fixed the slope b at 1, with amounts in the token's raw units.
lines.tts: But the analysis plan fixed the slope b at one, with amounts in the token's raw units.

lines.sub: A raw unit, or base unit, is the smallest piece of a token. One USDC is one million base units.
lines.tts: A raw unit, or base unit, is the smallest piece of a token. One U S D C is one million base units.

lines.sub: Then any amount above 10 base units already gives V above 0.99991, less than one ten-thousandth below 1.
lines.tts: Then any amount above ten base units already gives V above zero point nine nine nine nine one, less than one ten-thousandth below one.

lines.sub: In the registered analysis, 99.52% of transfers had at least 10 base units.
lines.tts: In the registered analysis, ninety-nine point five two percent of transfers had at least ten base units.

lines.sub: So did 99.78% of latest allowances.
lines.tts: So did ninety-nine point seven eight percent of latest allowances.

lines.sub: So the amount played no part, and this is one of the reasons the amounts were later revised.
lines.tts: So the amount played no part, and this is one of the reasons the amounts were later revised.
